newsitem.title: UK: Church's "gay" debate set to spark controversy.
newsitem.headline: Church's "gay" debate set to spark controversy.

text.p: Church of England leaders and representatives gathered on Friday for a General Synod which will broach the controversial issue of homosexuality within the church.

London archdeacon David Gerrard has introduced a private member's motion entitled "Issues in Human Sexuality", which is scheduled for debate during Monday's session of the five-day meeting in York, in northern England.

Gerrard's motion has been supported by 180 members, guaranteeing it space on the synod's agenda. A representative of the Church of England was anxious to point out that the motion was on human sexuality in general and not purely the issue of homosexuality.
But since Gerrard announced his intention to introduce the motion in June, it has been described by him and others as an opportunity to discuss the matter of gay priests within the church.
Gerrard is not gay, left-wing or a sexual rights campaigner, but said he believed homosexuality and its role within the church was an important issue and one which needed to be aired.
The Church of England, consisting of around 80 million members worldwide, does not condemn homosexuality outright, but does not give its blesssing either.
The issue has not been discussed at a synod, the church's parliament, since a debate in 1981, when it was voted that "homosexual acts fall short of (God's) ideal."

The Church is more tolerant in matters of homosexuality than Roman Catholicism, which does not allow its priests to have sexual relations of any kind, but there are those within the Church of England who say it should still be considered a sin.

A spokesman for the Roman Catholic Church said: "We welcome this debate, which is misunderstood from the Church's point of view. We do not condemn homosexuals, but we are against sexual relations outside marriage and for all priests."
Feelings on the subject run high and it is likely to provoke passionate debate and threaten the fiercest controversy in the Church since the 1992 decision to ordain women priests.

The Lesbian and Gay Christian Movement said the debate was long overdue, but were sceptical about how much would actually be achieved because gay priests would be fearful of losing their jobs if they spoke from personal experience.

"We know of clergy who are members of the synod and who are gay, but have been told by the bishops that they can say goodbye to their jobs if they speak out," the Reverend Richard Kirker told Reuters.
"This can't be an open debate because the very people who should be speaking most are the very group who the church leadership have the greatest power to stop speaking."
"But as we saw with the ordination of women priests, changes of a significant nature can happen in the face of huge opposition, and this debate is a step in the right direction," Kirker said.
The synod is due to run to July 15 and other issues scheduled for debate include a motion on "Standards of Morality and Decency" and a discussion on the ethics of test-tube fertilisation.
